card st-ticket-own-checks  [decided]
Eight checks on one ticket, each read from the ticket file alone
why: A check that needs only the file can run as soon as the planner writes it, and its failure names exactly one ticket.
Each check reads one ticket file and nothing else. A ticket passes when it meets all eight:
- **title**: the file has a line `title: <text>` with non-empty text. A file with no title is not parsed, so no other check runs on it.
- **shape**: every header line and every section heading of the ticket format is present (#st-ticket-shape). A failure names each missing line or heading.
- **size**: the whole file, header and every section, is 4000 characters or fewer.
- **what-to-build**: the `## What to build` section has text. An empty section and a missing heading both fail.
- **acceptance**: the `## Acceptance criteria` section has at least one bullet, a plain `-` or a `- [ ]` checkbox.
- **no-file-paths**: the file names no file path, in the header or in the body. A path is a token with at least one `/` between two name characters that ends in a file extension (a dot and 1 to 5 letters or digits), for example `src/loop.ts` or `src/*.ts`. A `files:` line also fails. A URL, a bare file name such as `Makefile`, a slash command such as `/implement`, a card id, and a make target do not count. A failure lists each path with its line number.
- **make-targets**: every bullet under `## Checks` is `make <target>` (#lp-checks-scripts). An empty `## Checks` section passes, and the ticket then uses the rubric's default checks.
- **touches**: the `touches:` line names at least one module, and no name reads as a path. A name reads as a path when it holds a slash or a backslash, or ends in a file extension. This rule is stricter than no-file-paths, because a module name has no reason to hold either. The scheduler compares these names to decide which tickets build at the same time (#st-build-parallel).
`stories:` and `cites:` can be empty and still pass. A prefactor delivers no story (#st-ticket-stories). Whether the cards and stories are covered is a question about the whole set (#st-ticket-set-checks).
  -> refines         st-ticket  A ticket is a tracer-bullet slice of decided cards

card st-ticket  [decided]
A ticket is a tracer-bullet slice of decided cards
why: A decided card is a constraint, not a unit of work. A builder needs something narrow, complete, and small enough for one fresh context.
subtree: 11 cards, 11 decided, 1 unchallenged
A ticket is the unit of build work. It is a tracer bullet: a narrow but complete path through every layer the change touches. It can be shown working on its own, and it fits one fresh context.
A ticket is not a card. A card groups by decision, so a slice usually crosses several cards, and most cards are a constraint on a thing, not the thing.
A ticket holds a title, the end-to-end behaviour it makes work from the user's side, its acceptance criteria, the spec stories it delivers (#st-ticket-stories), the decided cards it cites, the tickets that block it, and the checks that decide it. The file format of these fields is fixed (#st-ticket-shape).
A ticket names no file paths. They go out of date before the build reaches the ticket.
blocked_by is the delivery order, and the planner decides it. It is not derived from the depends_on edges between the cited cards (#st-ticket-set-checks).
Two groups of checks decide whether a ticket set is valid (#lp-checks): the checks on one ticket (#st-ticket-own-checks) and the checks on the whole set (#st-ticket-set-checks).
#st-ticket-partial says what a failure of each group does to the board.
An agent writes the tickets from the spec (#st-spec). A person decides which ticket gets built, and when (#vi-board).

card st-ticket-checks-run  [decided]
The ticket checks run on their own as one operation with one verdict
why: A planner, a person and an agent that edits a ticket all need to run the same checks without a plan, and read the result as one verdict plus the place of each failure.
One operation runs every ticket check on a folder of tickets: the own checks on each ticket (#st-ticket-own-checks) and the set checks on the whole set (#st-ticket-set-checks). It needs the folder, the decided cards the tickets may cite, and the spec whose stories they deliver.
Each failure names its ticket, the check and the field. A set failure that no ticket owns names the set. The reader finds the place to fix without reading the rest of the output.
The verdict is the exit code, as for every check (#lp-checks). A pass, a failed check and a malformed call are three different outcomes, so a call that could not run the checks never reads as a pass.
The operation has no tool of its own in this card. Which program carries it is decided elsewhere.
